aspects.says: from/toInstant carry a moment and valueOf/toLocalDateTime a wall-clock value; a wall-clock column in a known zone is converted with that zone in java.time before valueOf.
basis: section:Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone

aspects.says: GregorianCalendar.from and toZonedDateTime keep the calendar's zone; toInstant drops it, so the zone attached next must be the calendar's own, not the JVM's default.
basis: section:A Calendar Converts With Its Own Zone, Not the JVM's

aspects.says: An Instant is compared with a Date at millisecond precision, truncating as Date.from does, never rounding and never with a tolerance.
basis: section:Date and Instant Name the Same Moment, but a Date Keeps Only Milliseconds

aspects.says: Date.from(Instant) keeps only milliseconds, so an Instant with digits below the millisecond does not equal its round trip through a Date, while Timestamp.from keeps nanoseconds.
basis: section:Date and Instant Name the Same Moment, but a Date Keeps Only Milliseconds

aspects.says: Timestamp.valueOf moves a wall-clock time in the default zone's DST gap forward and takes the later offset in an overlap, where atZone takes the earlier.
basis: section:Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone

aspects.says: GregorianCalendar.from gives ISO week rules, so WEEK_OF_YEAR can differ from a calendar built for a locale such as Locale.US.
basis: section:A Calendar Converts With Its Own Zone, Not the JVM's
aspects.reason: a test of it would depend on the locale a reader's calendar is built with; the page shows the run

aspects.says: JDBC 4.2 drivers take and return java.time types through setObject and getObject.
basis: section:Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone
aspects.reason: stated from the JDBC specification as a side note; no driver runs in the practices

aspects.says: Timestamp.valueOf, toLocalDateTime, java.sql.Date.valueOf and toLocalDate convert through the JVM's default zone, so the same values give different moments or dates under different default zones.
basis: section:Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone

aspects.says: Only GregorianCalendar has toZonedDateTime; any other Calendar converts with toInstant and getTimeZone().toZoneId().
basis: section:A Calendar Converts With Its Own Zone, Not the JVM's

aspects.says: Legacy three-letter IDs convert through toZoneId (EST to a fixed -05:00, PST to America/Los_Angeles), and ZoneId.of rejects them.
basis: section:Build a TimeZone from a ZoneId, So a Wrong ID Fails
aspects.reason: a lookup fact with no decision for a practice to grade; the reference table and the run show it

aspects.says: A java.sql.Date is midnight in the default zone of the JVM that made it, so its milliseconds read in a JVM in another zone can give another day.
basis: section:Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone

aspects.says: TimeZone.getTimeZone(String) turns an unknown ID into GMT, while TimeZone.getTimeZone(ZoneId.of(id)) rejects it.
basis: section:Build a TimeZone from a ZoneId, So a Wrong ID Fails
